text:
FPMC combines long-term personalization and directed transitions additively: s(u,i,j)=pᵤᵀqⱼ+aᵢᵀbⱼ, with separate source/destination embeddings permitting asymmetry; basket histories average the transition term. Its user–previous-item interaction is candidate-independent and cancels in ranking. TransRec instead couples personalization and sequential dynamics through s(u,i,j)=βⱼ−d(γᵢ+tᵤ,γⱼ), where tᵤ includes a global translation. Translation makes transitions directional; βⱼ captures popularity. Neither formulation requires observed pair counts at inference. Sources: [FPMC](https://www.ra.ethz.ch/cdstore/www2010/www/p811.pdf), [TransRec](https://ijcai.org/proceedings/2018/734).

Sparse item-to-item scoring typically takes s(H,j)=Σᵢ∈H w(H,i)Wᵢⱼ: personalization comes from history selection and recency weights, while directed W captures pairwise relationships. Sequential Rules estimates W using order-sensitive, distance-discounted counts; learned linear models fit item relationships instead. TALE additionally uses time intervals and popularity trends. These precedents suggest that adding asymmetric pairwise scores to personalized scores is established; a distinct-user-count gate on a SASRec residual is a narrower design distinction, not evidence of novelty by itself. Sources: [Sequential Rules](https://arxiv.org/abs/1803.09587), [TALE](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.07382).

Suggested controls for s=s_SASRec+λg(Cᵢⱼ)Aᵢⱼ: SASRec alone; ungated learned A; count-only Cᵢⱼ; SASRec plus counts; and normalized transitions P(j|i)=(Cᵢⱼ+αpⱼ)/(ΣₖCᵢₖ+α), optionally scored as log P(j|i)−β log pⱼ. Define Cᵢⱼ as distinct training users exhibiting i→j; pⱼ is training target popularity. Row normalization alone preserves last-item count rankings without smoothing. Match history windows, tune on macro validation HR@10, and compare symmetric versus asymmetric A and performance on zero-count pairs. These ablations distinguish count memorization, popularity correction, and learned generalization.
